issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Public Transport' is hard to justify from the rest of the profile. The triggers are auditory/name/voice reminders linked to childhood caregiver abuse, and the negative appraisals are shame/self-blame/meaninglessness. Avoiding public transport suggests a situational safety strategy tied to a specific external environment, but there are no threat, memory, or trigger items indicating transport-related danger, crowding, entrapment, or encounters with abuse reminders in that context. This makes the item clinically difficult to integrate with the rest of the selected profile and with the formulation, where maladaptive strategies are closely linked to triggers and appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more characteristically tied to sexual trauma and is difficult to reconcile as a central appraisal in this profile of childhood physical abuse without any supporting memory, trigger, or threat content suggesting bodily violation themes.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding evaluation of appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers childhood caregiver abuse with auditory/name/voice reminders and self-blame/meaning loss. This strategy is not well supported by the listed triggers or appraisals and feels aimed at a different symptom cluster than the rest of the profile.

vignette: Akua had always been a self-sufficient person, able to fix anything with her hands and face any challenge head-on. As a plumber, she took pride in being one of the few women in a male-dominated field. But it was this very independence that made her recent struggles all the more difficult to accept. Growing up, Akua had suffered at the hands of an abusive caregiver. The memories of those events were etched into her mind like scars on her skin. She tried not to think about them, but certain sounds – the creaking of a door, the rustling of fabric – would transport her back to that time and place. Hearing names similar to her abuser's or catching a glimpse of someone with a similar voice tone would send her spiraling into anxiety. Akua had come to believe that she was somehow to blame for what happened to her as a child. "If only I were stronger," she would tell herself, "if only I were more worthy." This self-doubt seeped into every aspect of her life. She felt like there was something fundamentally wrong with her, that she was defective in some way. Even the work she loved – fixing pipes and unclogging drains – no longer brought her joy. As a result, Akua began to avoid anything that reminded her of her abuser or the traumatic events of her past. She stopped attending family gatherings where she might encounter people with similar names or voices. She avoided authority figures, including police officers and healthcare professionals, fearing they would judge her or see right through her facade. When working on a job site, she would become anxious if someone with a similar voice tone was nearby. But these avoidance behaviors only served to reinforce Akua's negative self-image. The more she withdrew from the world, the more convinced she became that she was unfixable, that nothing in her life had meaning anymore. She started to ruminate on all the ways others had wronged her – including her abuser, but also people who were simply trying to help. "Why did they do this to me?" she would ask herself, getting lost in a cycle of resentment and self-pity. The consequences of these behaviors began to accumulate. Akua's relationships with her loved ones started to fray, as she became increasingly isolated and withdrawn. Her work suffered too – she was late to job sites, or would leave early, unable to shake off the feeling of unease that lingered long after she'd left a particular location. One day, while working on a particularly difficult plumbing job, Akua's anxiety became overwhelming. She had to take a break, stepping outside into the fresh air to calm herself down. It was then that she realized she couldn't keep living like this – constantly avoiding triggers, stuck in a cycle of self-blame and resentment. Something inside her shifted, and for the first time in years, Akua felt a spark of hope. Maybe, just maybe, it was time to confront her demons head-on, rather than running from them. With a newfound sense of determination, Akua made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to finally break free from the grip of her past and find meaning in her life once more.
